name: Scalloped Potato Turkey Casserole
writer_notes: SELECTOR: Sliced-potato gratin with turkey; catalog has no scalloped-potato bake at all and potatoes are the cheapest starch on the board. Source verified at 4-6 servings but prints no nutrition. Confidence: numbers unverified from source, est_cal computed from our ratios. | HARVEST: Source yield is stated as a range, "Serves 4 - 6"; midpoint 5 recorded.
intro_html: Scalloped potatoes are just thin potato slices baked in seasoned dairy until they collapse into layers. Add turkey and cheddar and it stops being a side dish and becomes dinner. Each serving carries 38 grams of protein and 562 calories for about $2.76 (at everyday cost). Potatoes are the cheapest thing in the produce section by a wide margin, and this pan uses most of a nine pound bag.
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Pantry seasonings (black pepper, salt): ~$0.52. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $24.30 across 14 servings, so roughly $1.74 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $31.78 across 14 servings, roughly $2.27 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $8.82 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $40.60. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About $2.76 a serving (at everyday cost). Nearly a third of the food weight in this pan is potato, which is exactly why the number lands where it does.
shop_smart: Buy the largest sack of potatoes the store sells. This bake runs through most of a 9 lb bag, and loose potatoes cost noticeably more per pound.
A mandoline is not required but a steady hand is. Even slices are the difference between creamy layers and a pan with raw spots, and thin slices cook faster and cost the same.
Milk plus eggs plus a little flour makes a custard that costs a fraction of what heavy cream does and sets firmer in a scalloped bake. There is no reason to buy cream for this.
One frozen turkey breast roast covers the whole pan. Roast it yourself rather than buying deli turkey, which runs several times the price per pound.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Slice the potatoes about an eighth of an inch thick, skins on or off as you prefer, and keep them in cold water until you are ready so they do not brown.
Whisk the milk, eggs, flour, Dijon mustard, salt, and plenty of black pepper together until completely smooth. This is the custard that holds the whole thing together.
Melt the butter with the garlic and stir it into the custard, which distributes the fat and garlic evenly instead of leaving pockets.
Drain and dry the potato slices, then layer a third of them into a greased and buttered 9x13 pan, followed by a third of the diced turkey breast and a scatter of cheddar.
Repeat the layers twice more, then pour the custard slowly over the top and press the whole thing down so the liquid works into every layer.
Cover with foil and bake at 375F for 50 minutes, then uncover, add the last of the cheddar, and bake 20 to 25 minutes more until the top is browned and a knife slides through with no resistance.
Rest 20 minutes before portioning. Scalloped potatoes need that time to firm up or they will slide apart on the spatula.
portion_html: Weigh the pan, subtract the empty pan weight, and divide by 14. Cut squares to the scale and lift them with a wide spatula so the layers stay stacked. Each serving comes to 562 calories and 38 grams of protein.
credit_html: Recipe adapted from 12tomatoes.com, rebuilt for 14-serving budget meal prep with weighed portions and Omaha pricing.
upsell_html: A layered potato and turkey bake for about $2.76 a serving (at everyday cost), and this is one of many. Members get every recipe in the Meal Prep section, plus the full library of money lessons, calculators, and tools, for $1 a month.

head.description: Scalloped potato turkey casserole meal prep: thin potato layers with turkey and cheddar in a Dijon custard. 562 calories, 38g protein, about $2.76 a serving (at everyday cost).
head.keywords: scalloped potato casserole, turkey potato bake, leftover turkey recipes, cheap potato dinner, high protein casserole, budget meal prep
steps: Slice the potatoes an eighth of an inch thick and hold them in cold water.
Whisk the milk, eggs, flour, Dijon, salt, and pepper smooth, then stir in the garlic butter.
Layer drained potatoes, diced turkey, and cheddar into a greased 9x13 pan three times over.
Pour the custard over the top, press down, cover with foil, and bake at 375F for 50 minutes.
Uncover, add the last cheddar, bake 20 to 25 minutes more, rest 20 minutes, and portion into 14 containers.
